newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia experiment extends domestic bond maturities.
newsitem.headline: Russia experiment extends domestic bond maturities.

text.p: Russia's central bank and finance ministry radically extended the maturities of the domestic bond market on Wednesday, with the announcement that bonds running for up to eight years would go on sale.
But the authorities made clear the new issues were to be seen as an economic experiment to lengthen the yield curve rather than a fund-raising exercise.

Although the central bank and finance ministry are more optimistic than market participants about demand for the new paper, they acknowledge it will take half a year for interest in the new market to unfold.

Starting on July 31 the central bank will offer five OFZ bond issues from its portfolio. Each pays annual interest of 10 percent, with maturities running from four to eight years. The total volume of the issues is 30.71 trillion roubles.
The longest paper currently in circulation is a three-year OFZ bond maturing in June 2000.
"We are giving the market a new long-term instrument, so that participants can form long-term perspectives," bank first deputy chairman Sergei Aleksashenko told Reuters.

"We don't intend to sell these 30 trillion roubles of bonds tomorrow or over a short period. But we think that we shouldn't keep government debt in short maturities, and we have to give the market an opportunity to get used to long paper," he said.
The bonds are restructured from part of the 80.4 trillion roubles in direct credits given by the central bank to the finance ministry to fund the budget deficit in 1992-94.
The debt was restructured on March 15 this year into 13 OFZ bond issues with maturities from four to 16 years, and they are now held in the central bank's portfolio.
Starting on Thursday the central bank will quote selling prices for the five issues based on a yield of 17.5 percent, including accruals.
Bella Zlatkis, head of the securities and financial markets department in the finance ministry, said the bonds would be sold "not to raise any additional money but for macro-economic analysis".

Aleksashenko said the fact that the central bank was selling the bonds, rather than having them auctioned directly by the finance ministry, meant that sales could be flexible and in small amounts, to allow the market to get used to the new paper.
"If we sell this paper it will be purely to sterilise excess money supply, but that is not our aim," he said.
Traders said there was currently no demand for the paper, because of the currency risk, but interest would grow as yields on other issues fall.

Yields on taxable bills and bonds had fallen to 18.0 percent at the end of July from 19.5 percent at the end of June and 30.0 percent at the end of April. The longest three-year fixed-rate 20 percent bond currently yields 19.75 percent.

"The issue of these bonds can be taken as a signal from the central bank about a further decline in yields and an orientation plan for the next half year," said Andrei Vetrov, analyst at Moscow Narodny.

There was a danger in missing the opportunities offered by the bonds, he said, recalling how there had been little interest in the new three-year 20 percent fixed-rate OFZ bonds issued earlier this year, until a fall in market yields suddenly made them extremely attractive.
CSFB Moscow vice-president Sergei Koshelenko said non-resident investors would not be interested in such long maturities, as long as current T-bill yields remain stable.

"Either their price will become very cheap, or we will see a sharp fall in T-bill yields, or the rouble-dollar forward market will develop adequately. So far these three things haven't happened, so I see no reason to buy these bonds," he said.
But if investors think T-bill and shorter OFZ yields will fall, then the long end of the yield curve will offer the best returns, dealers said.
"The most risk-ready non-resident investors have already analysed the rouble situation and are not hedging their positions," said a trader at a bank in London.
"From talks with clients and investors I know that many are interested in just such long paper," he said.
